title: Reusing a node pool vs destroying and recreating nodes
variable: pool reuse vs destroy/create per cycle
claim: Gameface RAG 07-performance.md, 'Node Pooling for High-Frequency Elements' (SEVERITY: high): 'Creating and destroying DOM nodes rapidly (particle-style notifications, damage numbers, loot pop-ups) forces repeated parsing, style resolution, and layout.' perf-lint.ts lists node pooling among the patterns it cannot check statically, so the recommendation currently ships without a number attached. This case supplies it.
result: Confirmed, and strongly - but on a different axis than hypothesized, which rule 10 says is worth a note. Expected Layout; the dominant cost is Styles: 6.11x at 30, 8.90x at 100, 8.19x at 300, while Layout stayed at 1.04-1.22x and fell below the guardrail at 100 and 300. The reading is that in cohtml the expensive part of recreating a node is resolving its style from scratch, not laying it out - layout runs over the same node count either way, but a pooled node keeps its resolved style and a fresh one does not. That sharpens the RAG guidance: 'forces repeated parsing, style resolution, and layout' is right to list style resolution, and this case says style resolution is the term that dominates.
notes: Applicability gate: ADAPTED. createElement/removeChild/appendChild/textContent were verified manually against the Player. THE ADAPTATION, and why: the spec frames this as 'per cycle'. The lab reports steady-state MEDIANS over a 5s window, so a low-duty-cycle spawn burst would fall outside the median and both variants would report their idle cost - a false NO RELIABLE DIFFERENCE. The refresh therefore runs every frame in both variants. Read the ratio as 'what pooling saves per refresh', not as 'what a damage-number system costs'. Rule 1: one variable, whether the elements are reused or replaced. Rule 2: identical DOM at the end of every frame - same node count, same classes, same positions, same text. Rule 3: identical JS apart from the single USE_POOL constant; both pages define both paths, both build the initial set the same way, and both maintain the tiles array. Rule 4: identical text - the label derives from the frame counter and the index, so both variants render the same strings of the same lengths at the same moment. Rule 5: 300 tiles occupy 1852x1032 inside 1920x1080. Rule 6: the churn replaces the damage driver and starts at load with no idle window. Rule 7: no randomness. Rule 8: counts 30/100/300. Rule 9: plain HTML/CSS/JS. Rule 10: expected axis is Layout, with Styles plausible too since recreated nodes must have their styles resolved from scratch; a Styles-dominant result would be worth a note rather than a failure.
